visits.text: Turtle museum (ext) — Natural/urban highlight with context.

The Bandrélé salt ecomuseum showcases the work of the “mamas shingo” (salt mothers in Shimaoré). These salt-makers gather silt from the mangrove and turn it into brilliantly white salt by cooking it over a wood fire.
Saziley trailhead — Scenic geological or heritage feature.
Bandrélé salt does not come from evaporating seawater but from boiling the brine concentrated in the silt. This ancestral technique of Bantu origin is passed down from mother to daughter.
Coastal promontories — Classic viewpoint for photos.
Sakouli Beach, on the east coast facing the lagoon, is lined with century-old baobabs. The largest need about thirty people to encircle them.
Facing Sakouli, Bandrélé Islet stands out for its coral reef teeming with life. It can be reached by kayak or paddleboard from the beach.
Heading south, Mont Choungui rises in a perfect cone to 594 m. Its basalt silhouette can be seen from Petite-Terre and dominates the whole southern part of the island.

N'Gouja beach is the most famous on Mayotte, about forty minutes' drive from Bandrélé. Fine sand under baobabs and tropical almond trees, green turtles grazing on the seagrass a few meters from the shore, and lemurs in the branches.
Southern beaches loop — Natural/urban highlight with context.

From the village of Mtsamoudou, the Saziley trail winds in among the baobabs. The site holds nearly 700 of them, including the African baobab and the very rare Malagasy baobab (6 of the 7 specimens found in Mayotte).
Coral rubble flats — Scenic geological or heritage feature.
Pointe Saziley is the driest spot in Mayotte, with only three humid months. Its 3-million-year-old volcanic relief forms the shape of a crocodile's head when seen from above.
Turtle observation points — Classic viewpoint for photos.
Ten beaches host green turtles for nesting at the Saziley site. An estimated 1,500 nestings occur each year. Females come ashore to lay between 100 and 150 eggs after nightfall.
The padzas — patches of heavily eroded red earth — carve the landscape into natural amphitheaters. This phenomenon typical of southern Mayotte stands out sharply against the green vegetation.
Offshore, Îlot de Sable Blanc rises from the lagoon. This tiny sandbank serves as a refuge for terns, whose plumage blends with the whiteness of the coral sand.
The coral reef 50 meters from Saziley beach is exceptional: corals of varied shapes and colors, sheltering a wealth of life.

activities.text: Visit the salt ecomuseum with a demonstration by mamas shingo: silt harvest, filtration in perforated basins, cooking, and packaging. Leave with a bag of artisan salt.
Snorkeling at N'Gouja, about forty minutes' drive from Bandrélé: step into the clear water and swim with the green turtles peacefully grazing on the gently sloping seagrass beds.
Kayak or paddleboard to Bandrélé Islet. The fringing reef shelters hard corals, butterflyfish, and starfish.
Hike the Saziley trail from Mtsamoudou. The GR1 crosses the site on 21 km of marked paths, among baobabs, beaches, and padzas.
Supervised bivouac to observe turtle nesting after dark. Coastal Conservancy rangers accompany visitors in silence to the beaches.
Snorkeling off Saziley beach, where the fringing reef begins a few meters from shore. Parrotfish, damselfish, and moray eels are common.

visits.text: Dziani crater lake rim — Natural/urban highlight with context.
Lake Dziani Dzaha fills a volcanic crater extinct for about 7,000 years. Its emerald-green waters contain cyanobacteria and are corrosive: swimming is prohibited. A marked trail circles it in 1h15.
Plage de Moya cliffs — Scenic geological or heritage feature.
From the crater rim, the panorama stretches over Grande-Terre, the lagoon, and the Indian Ocean. In Mahorian, “dziani” means lake and “dzaha” crater.
Lighthouse point — Classic viewpoint for photos.
Descend to the Moya beaches, former collapsed craters forming near-circular coves open to the sea. This is a major sea turtle nesting site, monitored year-round.
The cliffs bordering Moya reveal the geological strata of past volcanic activity. The white-tailed tropicbird, a white bird with a long tail, nests in the rock faces.

Head back up to the historic quarter of the Rocher de Dzaoudzi. Here stands the Résidence des Gouverneurs, a metal-framed building constructed in 1891-1892 by the Moisant workshops, a rival of Eiffel. The building is a listed historic monument.

The MuMA (Musée de Mayotte) occupies the former barracks on the Rocher, on Place de France, a stone's throw from the barge landing. The building has been closed to the public for several years, weakened by earthquakes and then stripped of its roof by Cyclone Chido: check before you go, the colonial façade can be seen from the square.
Petite‑Terre coastal path — Natural/urban highlight with context.

Take the Boulevard des Crabes, an artificial causeway built in the early days of French colonization. It links the Rocher de Dzaoudzi to Pamandzi; before it was built, the town was cut off at high tide.
Old airstrip point — Scenic geological or heritage feature.
At low tide, a side trail leads to the Badamiers mudflats. Fiddler crabs, mangroves, and shorebirds populate this habitat between land and sea.
Lagoon viewpoints — Classic viewpoint for photos.
The Bagamoyo site, along the causeway, reveals a vast medieval cemetery dating from the 10th to 13th century. Muslim graves appear at low tide, remnants of a vanished village.
The Polé mosque preserves traces of one of Mayotte's oldest places of worship, predating the 19th century. It is also a site of animist rites, where locals come to invoke the djinns.
Climb up to the Vigie site, Petite-Terre's highest point at 202 m. The panorama takes in Grande-Terre, the airport runway, the Passe en S, and the turquoise waters of the lagoon.
Finish at Plage du Faré, the most accessible beach on Petite-Terre. Sunsets here are spectacular, with Mont Choungui as a backdrop.

activities.text: Hike the circuit around Lake Dziani and descend to Moya beaches. Marked trail, some woodland passages and a steep descent to the beach.
Snorkeling at Moya: crystal-clear water lets you observe corals and tropical fish right from the beach. Watch for currents on the ocean side.
Guided tour of Dzaoudzi's historic quarter with audio guide available in four languages. Pass by the Church of Saint-Michel (1849), the colonial hospital, and the first doctor's house.
Hike the GR1 on Petite-Terre: a 15-km circuit crosses from the Dziani natural site to Moya beaches, passing through the Vigie. Doable as a day hike or in stages.
Petite-Terre's Christian cemetery shelters majestic frangipani trees and tombs of former governors. Honoré de Balzac's brother, Henry, rests here.
Enjoy Badamiers beach for a voulé facing the lagoon. Clear views across to the Rocher de Dzaoudzi and Grande-Terre.

visits.text: Market and seafront — Natural/urban highlight with context.
Mamoudzou's covered market brings together fruit vendors, fishermen, and artisans under one roof. Mangoes, papayas, manioc, leafy greens, ginger, and zebu mingle in a joyful, colorful jumble.
Ferry jetty — Scenic geological or heritage feature.
Step inside the Church of Notre-Dame de Fatima, built in 1855 on the heights above town. It's one of only two Catholic places of worship in Mayotte, a territory that is 95% Muslim.
Hillside viewpoints — Classic viewpoint for photos.
Stroll along Rue du Commerce, Mamoudzou's main thoroughfare. The stalls mix textiles, spices, and Comorian crafts in a lively atmosphere.
The marina pier marks the starting point for sea outings: diving, whale watching (July to October), and excursions to the lagoon's islets.
Facing the pier, a sculpture honoring Zéna M'Déré recalls this emblematic figure of Mayotte's decision to remain within the French Republic.
Head to Pointe Mahabou Park, a botanical garden laid out as a fitness trail. Palms, coconut trees, tamarinds, and bougainvillea line the paths.

The Pointe Mahabou belvedere rises to 58 m and offers a panorama over the port, Petite-Terre, M'Bouzi Islet, and the lagoon. The tomb of Sultan Andriantsoly, the last sultan of Mayotte, who ceded the island to France in 1841, lies just below.
Coconut market — Natural/urban highlight with context.
The M'tsapéré district, south of Mamoudzou, retains a few buildings from the colonial era. The old white mosque of Balamanga and its minaret are the most visible remnants.
Craft stalls — Scenic geological or heritage feature.
Cross the mangrove along marked trails winding between mangrove trees and mudflats. Fiddler crabs wave their single oversized claw while mudskippers hop between the roots.
Coastal esplanade — Classic viewpoint for photos.

North of the center, Kawéni is Mamoudzou's main business district, with its shopping area and warehouses. Along the lagoon, the Kawéni mangrove spreads its mangrove trees, where crabs and herons appear at low tide.
From the shore, M'Bouzi Islet stands out in the middle of the lagoon. This 142-hectare national nature reserve shelters primary dry forest with Comoro ebony, an endangered species.
The remains of sugar mills dot the trails between Mamoudzou and Dembéni. Sugar made Mayotte's fortune in the 19th century, before the crisis of 1883-1885.
Head to Passamainty Waterfall, reached via a woodland trail. The trickle of water falls into a pool shaded by tropical vegetation.
Town murals — Natural/urban highlight with context.
Take the barge linking Mamoudzou to Petite-Terre. The crossing takes 15 to 20 minutes and offers sweeping views of both islands, the lagoon, and the reef.
Scenic geological or heritage feature.
Arriving on Grande-Terre, the waterfront reveals the port's daily bustle. Yellow barges shuttle nonstop between the two shores.
Farewell promenade — Classic viewpoint for photos.
The town hall square marks the administrative heart of the capital. The architecture blends colonial heritage with modern buildings.
Craving sand? Trévani Beach, in the municipality of Koungou north of Mamoudzou, is the closest to town. Light-colored sand and calm lagoon waters.
Back in town, the Maison de l'Artisanat displays jewelry, pottery, and basketry made by local craftspeople. The salouvas (traditional fabrics) compete in vibrant colors.

activities.text: Sample mataba (manioc leaves pounded with coconut milk) and chicken pilao at the covered market. Vendors serve quick meals from mid-morning onward.
Board a boat from the pier for snorkeling in the lagoon. Green turtles and colorful fish populate the seagrass beds just offshore.
In the evening, Mahoran families gather at the farés of Pointe Mahabou for voulé, the local open-air barbecue.
Explore the mangrove by kayak from the Mamoudzou coast. You'll paddle between walls of foliage hiding kingfishers and striated herons.
Dive clubs at the Mamoudzou pier offer introductory dives and trips to Passe en S, where currents and visibility attract rays, reef sharks, and schools of jacks.
Browse the market in late afternoon for spices (vanilla, turmeric, clove) and packets of poutou, the chili blend every cook prepares her own way.
Join a Sunday voulé if the calendar allows: Mahorans gather with family on the beaches, around fresh fish skewers and coconut rice.
Try wakeboarding or water skiing from the marina. The lagoon's sheltered waters are ideal for beginners.
In the evening, taste mabawas (grilled chicken wings) seasoned with poutou at waterfront eateries.

visits.text: Choizil islets views — Natural/urban highlight with context.
From the shore at Mtsamboro, the Choizil Islets stand out against the lagoon. Two islets untouched by any construction, linked by a strip of white sand that appears only at low tide.
Northern reef edge — Scenic geological or heritage feature.
The village of Mtsamboro sits on a rocky outcrop on the north coast. Its minarets rise above the low houses, facing the islet of the same name — the largest in Mayotte at 240 hectares.
Fishing village — Classic viewpoint for photos.
On the Grande-Terre side, the minarets of Hamjago and Mtsamboro stand out against the green mountains. On clear days, the island of Anjouan (Comoros) appears on the northwestern horizon.
Pointe Mkadijou, Mayotte's northernmost point, remains hard to access. Its dry thickets and preserved reefs form a wild landscape protected by the Conservatoire du littoral.
Along the coast, traditional pirogues are pulled up on the sand. The village fishermen set out at dawn and return with tuna, grouper, and jacks.

activities.text: Boat excursion to the Choizil Islets. Snorkel in turquoise, crystal-clear water among clownfish, angelfish, and multicolored corals.
From July through October, humpback whales and their calves frequent the waters around Mtsamboro Islet. Sea trips also offer dolphin watching year-round.
Picnic on the sandbar between the two Choizil Islets at low tide. A postcard setting with no human trace.

visits.text: Islet sandbank views — Natural/urban highlight with context.
Sada is built on a hillside on the west coast. Facing the village, Sada Islet connects to the beach by a tombolo — a natural sandbar passable at low tide.
Baobab groves — Scenic geological or heritage feature.
The town has eleven mosques, including two Friday mosques barely a hundred meters apart, unique in Mayotte. They bear witness to old rivalries between the districts of Gnambobolé and Gnambotiti.
Sunset viewpoints — Classic viewpoint for photos.
Place Ha Ndovou (Bakery Square) is the heart of the village. This is where gatherings, the market, and cultural events such as the debaa (women's religious dance) take place.
The Place de l'Artisanat displays jewelry, pottery, and basketry. Visitors can sometimes watch the mlidi (men's religious dance) or madjlissi performed at weddings.
South of the town, Tahiti Plage stretches its light-colored sand facing Bouéni Bay. The lagoon's calm waters invite snorkeling and lazing about.
The sunset from Sada is one of the finest in Mayotte. The Bouéni peninsula closes off the bay opposite, and the sun sinks into the Mozambique Channel.
Mangrove boardwalk — Natural/urban highlight with context.
In Combani, in the island's interior, rows of ylang-ylang trees line up their twisted branches. This six-petaled yellow flower is hand-picked every morning to preserve its fragrance.
Ylang distillery (exterior) — Scenic geological or heritage feature.
Ylang-ylang was introduced to Mayotte in the early 20th century. Its essential oil goes into the composition of great perfumes and is the pride of the island, nicknamed the “island of perfumes.”
Village lanes — Classic viewpoint for photos.
The Coconi botanical garden spreads out its rows of palms, coconut trees, and tropical plants. The nursery can also be visited, especially beautiful in the rainy season.
Continue on to the Tsingoni mosque, one of the oldest in France (16th century). The village was once the capital of the Sultanate of Mayotte.
Lake Karihani (dziani Karihani), Mayotte's only natural freshwater lake, is often covered with water lilies. Egrets, herons, and moorhens take refuge there.
Heading back down to the west coast, the mangrove of Bouéni Bay lines the road. The mangrove trees form a dense curtain between land and lagoon.

activities.text: Cross the tombolo to Sada Islet at low tide. You can circle it on foot in an hour, with views over the west coast and Bouéni bay.
Snorkeling at Tahiti Beach: fringing reef accessible from shore, with corals and green turtles grazing the seagrass beds.
The passes of Sada and Bouéni, to the southwest, are renowned for scuba diving. Moderate currents, soft corals, and schools of pelagic fish.
Join an immersion day on a ylang-ylang farm: flower picking, distillation, essential oil making, and a countryside lunch.
Explore the mangrove by kayak or traditional pirogue. Among the mangrove roots, you'll come across mudskippers, crabs, and Madagascar pond herons.
Gentle walk around Lake Karihani, near Tsingoni. The shaded trail loops the water in under an hour.
